The Ethical Considerations of Surveillance Technology

Surveillance technology has become an increasingly prevalent part of our lives, with the rise of security cameras, drones, and smart devices. While these technologies have undeniable benefits, there are also significant ethical considerations that must be addressed. In this paper, we will explore some of the key ethical issues surrounding surveillance technology.

One of the most fundamental ethical considerations surrounding surveillance technology is the issue of privacy. The use of surveillance cameras, for example, raises questions about who can access the footage and for what purposes. In many cases, the footage is recorded and stored without the knowledge or consent of those being monitored. This raises concerns about the potential misuse of this information, as well as the invasion of privacy.

Another key ethical issue is transparency. It is important that individuals have a clear understanding of when and how they are being monitored. If surveillance technology is being used in secret, this can lead to a sense of mistrust and suspicion. Furthermore, it can be difficult to hold those in power accountable if their actions are not transparent.

A related issue is the potential for abuse of surveillance technology. There have been numerous cases of governments using surveillance to monitor dissidents or political opponents. Similarly, employers have been known to use surveillance technology to monitor their employees' activities outside of work, potentially violating their privacy and free will.

Another important ethical consideration is the question of consent. In many cases, individuals are not asked for their consent to be monitored. This raises questions about the legitimacy of the monitoring and whether it is truly voluntary. In some cases, individuals may consent to be monitored in order to access certain services or benefits, but this consent may not be fully informed.

Finally, there is the question of the impact of surveillance technology on our society as a whole. Surveillance can create a sense of fear and mistrust among citizens, leading to a "surveillance state" where everyone is constantly monitored. This can have a chilling effect on freedom of expression and other fundamental rights.

In conclusion, surveillance technology raises a number of important ethical considerations. These include issues of privacy, transparency, potential for abuse, consent, and the impact on society as a whole. It is crucial that we carefully consider these issues as we continue to develop and implement surveillance technologies.

We sat together on the hillside waiting for the momentous occasion. Throughout written history, there had always been two suns. Muto, the big sun, carried with it light and heat. It brought life into the world and bathed us with a comforting warmth. It was a being of love, growth, and fertility. We, as a people, cherished the power that Muto brought to our lives. Then there was Jeru, the little sun. Constantly eclipsed by his older and larger brother. He was always fighting to share what he had with us, constantly following the oath of his sibling to bring his energy to our people. Older civilizations characterized Jeru as kind of an understudy, one who would take his brother's place one day. We did not know if Muto would move on to help other lands or if he he might die, forever leaving the sky dimmer in his absence. Whatever the case might be, we still loved Jeru as well, even if his contributions sometimes made things a little too warm. Together, they leapt through the sky, always chasing each other, and rarely letting the darkness fall on out lands. In modern times, though, we discovered that, as a solar system, we were unusual. Twin suns were not the common configuration, and many who had lived their lives here had never seen a sky without the brothers. Every hundred years, however, the chase gets out of hand, and both Muto and Jeru leave us for a time. In the early days, we assumed they got lost, needed a break, or simply hid from us as a joke. Today, we know that the sun's paths sometimes take them beyond our sky at the same time. And we sat, staring upward from the greass, watching the brothers slide away into the horizon. We watched as the sky began to fade from orange to pink. As the pair drifted beyond our sight, the halos of their light sparkled just beyond, and the sky began to take on shades of purple and blue. We all sat agape as the sky began to be swallowed by blues and blacks. Finally, Muto and Jeru were gone, leaving us with stars..... other suns of other galaxies. They sparkled like jewels in the darkness, and we stared like awed children at this once in a lifetime view. For the first time in a hundred years, night fell on the Land of Two Suns.

The best advice I have ever been given comes from one of my favorite childhood movies: The Lion King. As Simba lay depressed over the death of his father, his newly found friend Timon gave him some advice to cope with his loss. He said "Fauna Matt" (meaning 'no worries'). There is something profoundly remarkable about having no worries. The very concept is alien to our highly competitive world. As I entered my junior year, homework and stress increased dramatically. AP classes were unlike any other class I had ever encountered. Multiple-choice questions were taken to a whole new level of thinking and timed essays left me scrambling for words. Acute Pancreatitis: Expected Presentation vs. Actual Case Essay

Table of Contents
 1. Abstract
 2. Introduction
 3. Disease description
 4. Actual patient case
 5. Critical analysis and knowledge synthesis
 6. Conclusion
 7. References

Abstract

Pancreatitis is a disease that occurs when pancreatic enzymes are activated in the pancreas rather than the small intestine (Prior, 2009). The disease can be acute or chronic. This paper investigates the variation between the expected presentation and an actual case of acute pancreatitis. Main symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea (Balthazar, 2002). Most common causes include gallstones, alcohol and metabolic disorders (Markel, 2009). Patient history, blood tests, ERCP and CT scan are main components of AP diagnosis. Treatment is usually done by administration of fluids, pain management and treatment for nausea. The patient in the case study was a male aged 45 years old and had a history of elevated cholesterol levels which was being managed using atorvastatin. The patient was also a habitual drinker. The patient was admitted suffering from upper abdominal pain nausea and vomiting (Balthazar, 2002). None of the probable causes of AP were established during the first episode. However, a mild lesion established during the second episode was able to confirm that the patient was suffering from acute pancreatitis associated with alcohol use. The patient was treated with meperidine to control pain in both episodes. Other non pharmacological therapies such as bowel rest and fluid replacement were offered.

There is a lot of literature concerning alcohol use and pancreatitis, however, the actual mechanism of interaction remains unknown. More research should be carried out to establish the missing information to improve the diagnosis of alcoholic pancreatitis.

Introduction

Pancreatitis can be described as a “disease that occurs when pancreatic enzymes are activated in the pancreas rather than the small intestine” (Markel, 2009, p. 1). Pancreatitis can occur due to several factors and result into varied symptoms. Acute pancreatitis can be described as a sudden attack that causes inflammation of the pancreas which is often associated with a severe upper abdominal pain (Prior, 2009). This paper seeks to compare and contrast expected presentation of the disease process and use of pharmacotherapeutics with the presentation and treatment witnessed with an actual patient case. The knowledge gained about the disease and drug treatment will then be synthesized through the creation of an appropriate case study of the selected disease process (Balthazar, 2002). In order to bring out a clear comparison only one form of pancreatitis (acute pancreatitis) will be discussed.

Disease description

As shown earlier, acute pancreatitis can be described as a sudden inflammation of the pancreas. Acute pancreatitis can have varied symptoms, the most common ones being: severe epigastric pain that radiates to the back; nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and loss of appetite; hemodynamic instability that may include shock; respiratory distress; tachycardia; and peritonitis (Balthazar, 2002).

The most common cause of acute pancreatitis include: gallstones; alcohol; metabolic disorders such as hereditary pancreatitis, hypercalcemia, hyperlipidemia and malnutrition; penetrating ulcers; abdominal trauma; malignancy; drugs such as steroids, sulfonamides, furosemides, thiazides; infections such as mumps, coxsackievirus, mycoplasma pneumoniae, ascaris and clonorchis; structural abnormalities such as choledochocele and pancreas divisum (Markel, 2009).

Other causes that are less common include long common duct; head and pancreas carcinomas; blockage of pancreatic flow by “ascaris; ischemia following bypass surgery; fatty necrosis;pregnancy; regular marathon running; cystic fibrosis; valproic acid; and aneroxia” (Prior, 2009, pp. 3).

In the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis, the physician requests for patient history regarding alcohol consumption and symptoms of gallstones. Blood tests are then ordered to confirm the cause of the symptoms. Laboratory tests that might be used in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis include: serum amylase and lipase; liver function tests; blood calcium tests; blood glucose tests; complete blood count and urinalysis; chest and abdominal x-ray; ultrasound examination; endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatology (ERCP); and computed tomography (CT) scan (Tsigrelis & Pitchumoni, 2006).

To treat AP, the patient is hospitalized, and an intravenous administration of fluids is carried out to assist in the restoration of blood volume (Prior, 2009). Medication for pain and nausea are provided to ease symptoms (Markel, 2009). Food consumption is usually withheld until the symptoms have been completely suppressed. Antibiotics are usually prescribed in severe cases of acute pancreatitis (Enns & Baillie, 1999). Alcohol consumption should be discontinued even if it’s found not to be the cause of the disease. If gall stones are identified to be the main cause of the acute pancreatitis then the gall bladder should be removed to prevent future episodes. In patients who the cause has not been directly identified, other diagnostic testing should be carried out. Worldwide statistics indicate that gallstones are the commonest causes of acute pancreatitis (AP).

Actual patient case

A “male patient aged 45 years who suffers from elevated cholesterol levels visited the hospital complaining of upper abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting for five days ” (Chintanaboina, & Gopavaram, 2012). The patient did not indicate any history of intolerance to drugs. Prior to the presentation the patient had began to take atorvastatin to manage the cholesterol. The patient was admitted to regular alcohol consumption. Investigations conducted on admission established that his vital signs were stable with a remarkable upper abdominal pain. Liver enzymes such as bilirubin were found to be normal. The serum lipase and amylase were elevated three times above the normal level (Enns & Baillie, 1999).

A CT scan indicated a mild edema of the pancreas. The findings were similar to those established in patients suffering from acute pancreatitis. An ultrasound was conducted on the abdomen indicated that the patient had a normal biliary tree (Markel, 2009). Atorvastatin treatment was temporarily stopped when the patient was admitted. The patient was treated with intravenous fluids, bowel rest, and pain management and discharged from the hospital three days after showing remarkable improvement (Chintanaboina, & Gopavaram, 2012, p. 5). On discharge, his serum lipase level had gone back to the normal range and he had begun to tolerate normal diet. No correlation was directly established between acute pancreatitis and atorvastatin therapy or alcohol use. The patient was however advised to cut down on his alcohol consumption and atorvastatin was restarted at the time of discharge. The risks associated with alcohol consumption and atorvastatin use were discussed with the patient before he was discharged to go home.

The same patient was re-admitted two months later with same symptoms. Upon examination, it was established that his vital signs were stable with a remarkable physical examination for upper abdominal tenderness (Balthazar, 2002 ). His serum amylase and lipase levels were raised considerably. A CT scan showed that there was a slight acinar atrophy and fibrosis (Balthazar, 2002). The slight pancreatic mass lesion could be attributed to alcohol use (Prior, 2009). The patient indeed confirmed that he had continued to take alcohol after the first visit. Further differential investigations were carried out to rule out other possible causes. Findings “on serum IgG4 levels were within the normal range and this ruled out the possibility of autoimmune pancreatitis” (Chintanaboina, & Gopavaram, 2012). The patient responded well to “bowel rest, intravenous fluids and pain management” (Balthazar, 2002, p. 6). In both cases pain control was achieved by meperidine adminstration. Investigation conducted on the levels of serum lipase and amylase showed that the two had gone down considerably. Following a thorough review of the patient case, no direct evidence was established between atorvastatin use and the acute pancreatitis. Alcohol use was implicated due to the fact that the damage established during the second visit was consistent with those established in other alcohol related cases. The patient was therefore advised to stop alcohol consumption. Atorvastatin therapy was again restarted upon discharge from the hospital. No more episodes of chronic pancreatitis were experienced by the patient in the two months follow up.

Critical analysis and knowledge synthesis

The findings of the above case are consistent with expected presentation of the disease process of acute pancreatitis. The symptoms that have been identified in the above case (Upper abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting) are some of the commonest symptoms of acute pancreatitis (Chintanaboina, & Gopavaram, 2012). However, the identification of these symptoms is not conclusive as there are many other conditions that have such symptoms. As described in medical literature concerning the disease, all the differential investigations carried out during the first visit did not show a possible cause of acute pancreatitis. The recurrence of the disease within two months led to a keen interest in establishing the possible cause. The patient was on atorvastatin therapy and was also a habitual alcohol user. There is no enough evidence on the association between pancreatitis and statin therapy. The case, therefore, offers a challenge to the dominant literature regarding the evidence of alcohol to induce pancreatitis.

Literature searches coupled with the findings of the above case has facilitated the organization information regarding alcohol use and acute pancreatitis.

According to the available data, alcohol abuse continues to be a major cause of morbidity and the mortality around the world (Markel, 2009). The association between alcohol use and pancreatitis is not very well understood as compared to the association between alcohol and other well known diseases such as liver cirrhosis. A census carried out in the United States showed that pancreatitis causes an estimated 5,000 deaths annually. Out of this figure, acute pancreatitis accounts for approximately 85%, with the remaining 15% attributed to chronic pancreatitis (Prior, 2009). Chronic pancreatitis is more commonly associated with alcohol abuse compared to acute pancreatitis.

There is lack of strong evidence to link pancreatitis with alcohol abuse. For instance, research data indicates that less than 10% of all alcohol abusers develop clinically relevant inflammation of the pancreas (Enns & Baillie, 1999). It’s therefore assumed that certain individuals are more at risk of developing chronic pancreatitis compared to others. Initially, alcohol abuse was only associated with chronic cases of pancreatitis that often resulted into endocrine and exocrine dysfunction (Markel, 2009). However, as shown in the above case, alcohol abuse can result acute pancreatitis. The acute exacerbations caused by alcohol can be detected early to prevent disease progression into the chronic phase.

A lot of research has been carried out in regard to the link between alcohol and chronic pancreatitis. However, the pathophysiology is still being investigated and there is no proper explanation for the mechanism. A study conducted by the University of Liverpool once concluded that acute pancreatitis occurs due to the fact that alcohol stimulates the pancreas into the production of fatty acids and other substances (Enns & Baillie, 1999). Such substances have the ability to destroy cells and inhibit the capacity of the pancreas to produce its own energy. Available literature indicates that the occurrence of the pancreatitis associated with alcohol often takes place in men aged between 35 and 40 years (Prior, 2009). The initial disease presentation may take several years to appear and usually increases when alcohol consumption is increased or taken for a prolonged period. The patient in the current case experienced pancreatitis symptoms for about one week. Studies indicate that pain experienced in chronic pancreatitis often resolves in one week (Balthazar, 2002).

Usually, the treatment of acute pancreatic is designed according to the needs of a given patient, and depending on the symptoms. The patient in the current case was treated with intravenous fluids, bed rest and pain management. In majority of acute pancreatitis cases, treatment is offered through supportive care, which may include bowel rest, pain killers, replacement of lost fluids and abstinence from food consumption (Balthazar, 2002). The therapy offered aims at preventing the development of further systemic complications, such as the necrosis of pancreatic tissue. The patient in the above case study was treated with meperidine to control pain. Historically, meperidine has been used as a first line option in controlling pain during an episode of acute pancreatitis (Markel, 2009). This is due to the fact that other narcotics were thought to cause irritation of the pancreas due to increased levels of lipase and amylase. However, recent research has shown that narcotic treatment does not necessarily result into increased release of pancreatic enzymes. Following this establishment any analgesic can be used in the treatment of acute pancreatitis. These include morphine, hydromorphine and meperidine (Markel, 2009). Meperidine is still commonly used in the treatment of pancreatitis though it usually has a dosage ceiling (Prior, 2009). Apart from pain control, treatment also aims at managing complications such as necrosis of the pancreatic tissue and organ failure. In the current case, this was done using intravenous fluid administration. This method is however not well understood, especially in regard to alcohol induced pancreatitis (Markel, 2009).

Conclusion

This paper sought to compare and contrast expected presentation of acute pancreatitis process and use of pharmacotherapeutics with the presentation and treatment witnessed with an actual patient case. A critical analysis of the pathophysiologic and pharmacotherapeutic components of an actual client case has also been conducted (Chintanaboina, & Gopavaram, 2012). The knowledge gained about the disease and drug treatment has been synthesized through the creation of an appropriate case study of the selected disease process.

It has been established that alcohol induced acute pancreatitis is not very well understood (Markel, 2009). Following the findings of this report, it’s recommended that more research should be carried out to establish the exact mechanisms through which alcohol results into pancreatitis. If this is established then repeated cases of attack can be prevented through proper diagnosis of alcoholic pancreatitis.

“The Caretaker” by Anthony Doerr Essay

The Caretaker by Anthony Doerr is a moving and shocking tale of Joseph, who lives in war-torn Liberia and finds himself in the USA, Oregon. This is a story of seeking redemption, struggle, and forgiveness with the self. The theme of isolation and loneliness comes out in this story. Civil war breaks out in Liberia, home of Joseph Saleeby. He loses everything that a man treasures and holds firmly to, his mother, country, and Way of life.

Liberia descends to anarchy and lawlessness, and he runs for dear life and finds himself in a different country, thousands of miles from his. He is on his own, with no relatives or government to call his own. He experiences a new culture, and this leaves him feeling alienated.

This is further worsened by his haunted and violent memories. He was forced to kill a rebel, saw decapitated children, rape, and other unimaginable crimes meted on his countrymen. He has no one to open his heart to, to tell his story; for a story shared is a story half solved? This tears him apart inside. He is a tormented soul who is emotionally isolated. His situation worsens when he loses his job and has nowhere to go.

However, the simple act of burying the hearts of whales and tending to a garden gives him the much needed inner peace he saw desires. He feels as if he has acquired a new lease of life. Belle, a deaf girl, is lonely and depressed and contemplates committing suicide.

She forms a unique friendship with Joseph and dissuades her from committing suicide. Theirs is a story of a confrontation with the self, isolation, and redemption. Haunted by isolation and loneliness in their respective struggles in life, they bond closely. Due to their plight, they create a strong and instant bond, a bond arising from need and not luxury. There’s a particular language, a language of the heart, and this helps them direct their paths of life in the right Way.

College. A single word with an infinite number of definitions. It is a place to further their intelligence, to take courses that they have never heard of before, to gain experience in fields not possible in high school. To some, it is a place they attend strictly for educational purposes. Their goals are to attain knowledge and skill for the success of their future. To others, it is the epitome of freedom, unrestrained by the rules of their parents and capable of deciding what they want to do. To me, it is a second home. Education is of course a priority and freedom is enjoyable, but what completes the college life is the environment a student lives in. What good is a college with superb education, but with a dull and heavy environment? What good is unlimited freedom when peers are not focused on the main reason for coming to college and just enjoying themselves? A perfect environment would be of one that is strict enough to keep me motivated to trying my best, while being loose enough to let me breathe and enjoy college life. So why Carnegie Mellon University, a university that is known to have a rigorous curriculum and exceptionally hardworking students? I know firsthand what a welcoming place it is. Because of my brother, a currently attending student, I have been to Carnegie Mellon countless times, mostly to drop him off or pick him up, but also for several college tours. I even got to meet some of the DA's, students, and faculty members due to my numerous visits and connections through my brother. Although I have toured a handful of colleges, none were as welcoming and warm as Carnegie Mellon. Although the school itself may be considered small in population relative to others, it does not lose in its vitality and enthusiasm in all aspects. It is professional enough to encourage students, but not so much as to discourage them. Out of the students that I have met, not a single person has said that they do not enjoy Carnegie Mellon; everyone was and is proud to be a Carnegie Mellon student or alumnus. My affinity for the university only strengthened. Carnegie Mellon has a superb Business school. US News (usnews.com) ranked Carnegie Mellon as #23 nationally, and #9 in the "Best Undergraduate Business Programs". The reason I am interested in business particularly is because of how I grew up. As both my parents are business majors, my father in economics and my mother in accounting, it was not unusual to hear conversations about the economy from an early age. Those conversations initially sparked my interest; I was curious enough to question what they were talking about and even voice my own opinions, although I was only a child and nowhere old enough to fully comprehend. As I grew up and moved from South Korea to the United States, I learned both the similarities and differences of the economic system in both countries. As we entered into the worldwide financial crisis that still affects us today, my family was greatly affected. Because my father recently changed his job, his pay was noticeably lessened. With a four-person family, and one child going to college soon, a decline in available expenses was inevitable. I know first-hand how it feels to go from having some economic freedom to being limited by a budget within a short period of time. I want to major in business not only for my own future but for the futures of others. Although I personally went through an economic crisis of my own, I am also aware that my problems are microscopic compared to others'. I believe I could be a pioneer to helping to resolve the financial crisis in the future. Attending Carnegie Mellon University, a university that is famous for its outstanding business program, would make that dream a reality.

The advent of nanotechnology has revolutionized numerous industries, leading to the production of a wide array of innovative consumer products. The integration of nanomaterials and nanoparticles into these products has resulted in significant advancements in performance, functionality, and efficiency. However, the rapid development and production of nanotechnology-based consumer items have also raised important concerns regarding their potential impact on health and safety. This paper aims to explore the profound impact of nanotechnology on consumer products, as well as the associated safety considerations and challenges.

The integration of nanotechnology into consumer products has led to the creation of an array of products with enhanced properties. For instance, nanotechnology has significantly improved the performance of clothing materials, leading to the production of wrinkle-resistant, stain-resistant, and water-repellent fabrics. Additionally, nanotechnology has enabled the development of high-performance sports equipment, such as lightweight and strong bicycles, golf clubs, and tennis rackets. Moreover, it has also facilitated the creation of advanced electronics, including flat-screen televisions and energy-efficient lighting sources.

The incorporation of nanotechnology in personal care products has also led to significant advancements. Nanoparticles have been utilized in the production of sunscreens, cosmetics, and skin care products, resulting in improved sun protection and skin moisture retention. Furthermore, nanotechnology has enabled the development of more efficient drug delivery systems, enabling the targeted delivery of medications to specific areas of the body, resulting in improved therapeutic efficacy and reduced side effects.

Despite the many advancements and benefits associated with the integration of nanotechnology in consumer products, there are also significant safety concerns that warrant careful consideration. The properties of nanomaterials are highly dependent on their size, shape, and chemical composition, which can result in adverse health effects when ingested, inhaled, or exposed to the skin. The small size of nanoparticles can enable them to cross cell membranes, leading to potential toxicity in various tissues and organs. Furthermore, the production and use of nanomaterials can lead to the generation of reactive oxygen species, which can cause oxidative stress and inflammation, contributing to the development of chronic diseases.

The environmental impact of nanotechnology is also a matter of concern. Nanoparticles are persistent and can accumulate in the environment, leading to the contamination of air, water, and soil. Moreover, the small size of nanomaterials can enable them to cross biological barriers and enter the food chain, potentially leading to adverse environmental and health effects. The release of nanoparticles from consumer products during the production, use, and disposal stages can also result in environmental pollution and pose threats to both human and ecological health.

In summary, the integration of nanotechnology in consumer products has resulted in significant advancements in performance, functionality, and efficiency. However, the rapid development and production of nanotechnology-based products have also raised important concerns regarding their potential impact on health and safety, as well as the environment. To address these challenges, there is a need for rigorous research and regulatory oversight to ensure that the benefits of nanotechnology are harnessed responsibly, while minimizing potential risks.

Title: The Importance of Extracurricular Activities in a Comprehensive Education

Imagine a world where students are not only confined to the boundaries of their textbooks, but are also provided with the opportunity to explore their interests outside the classroom. This is the world that our principal aims to create by enforcing a policy requiring all students to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. This decision has sparked a great deal of conversation and debate, with some arguing that students should be able to choose their extracurricular activities, while others believe that mandatory participation is essential for a well-rounded education. Having carefully considered both sides of the argument, I firmly stand in support of the principal's decision.

One of the primary reasons for supporting mandatory extracurricular participation is the vast array of benefits it provides for students' personal development. By engaging in activities such as sports, yearbook, or student council, students are encouraged to develop a sense of responsibility, leadership, and teamwork. These skills are not only crucial for their academic success, but also play a significant role in shaping their character and preparing them for future challenges in life.

For example, students participating in sports learn the importance of dedication, perseverance, and discipline. They learn to set goals, work hard to achieve them, and face the challenges that come their way with courage and resilience. On the other hand, students who work on the yearbook gain valuable experience in communication, creativity, and organization. They learn to collaborate with their peers, express their ideas, and manage their time effectively. Lastly, those who serve on the student council are given the opportunity to develop their leadership skills, make important decisions, and represent the interests of their fellow students.

Another compelling reason for supporting mandatory extracurricular participation is the fact that it encourages students to explore their interests and discover their passions. In a traditional classroom setting, students are often limited to learning within the confines of a prescribed curriculum. However, by participating in extracurricular activities, students are given the freedom to explore new horizons and discover their unique talents and interests. This not only enriches their educational experience, but also helps them to develop a sense of purpose and direction in life.

Moreover, mandatory extracurricular participation fosters a sense of community and belonging among students. By engaging in activities together, students are given the opportunity to build meaningful relationships with their peers and develop a strong sense of camaraderie. This sense of belonging is essential for promoting a positive school environment, enhancing students' overall well-being, and fostering a spirit of cooperation and collaboration among the student body.

In conclusion, the principal's decision to require all students to participate in at least one extracurricular activity is a wise and well-intentioned policy. By doing so, students are not only provided with the opportunity to develop essential life skills, but also given the chance to explore their interests and discover their passions. Furthermore, mandatory extracurricular participation fosters a sense of community and belonging among students, ultimately enriching their educational experience and preparing them for the challenges of the future. For these reasons, I strongly believe that all students should be encouraged to participate in at least one extracurricular activity, and I urge my fellow students and the school community to support this decision.

Invasive species are a growing concern in the world today, due to the significant impact they have on native ecosystems. These alien species, such as plants and animals, are often introduced by humans either intentionally or unintentionally, and they can cause a range of ecological, economic, and social problems. The introduction of invasive species can lead to changes in species composition, disruption of food webs, and even the extinction of native species. This essay will discuss the various ways in which invasive species affect native ecosystems and the measures that can be taken to mitigate their impact.
One of the main ways invasive species affect native ecosystems is through competition for resources. Invasive species often grow faster, reproduce more quickly, and are better adapted to the new environment than native species. They can outcompete native species for sunlight, water, nutrients, and other resources, leading to a decline in the abundance and diversity of native species. For example, the introduction of the zebra mussel into the Great Lakes has led to a decline in the population of native mussels due to competition for substrate and food.
Invasive species can also alter ecosystem processes, disrupting the delicate balance that exists between different species and their environment. For example, the introduction of the Chinese tallow tree into the southeastern United States has led to changes in the soil chemistry, which can inhibit the growth of native species. Invasive species can also alter fire regimes, which can have a cascading effect on the entire ecosystem. For instance, the introduction of cheatgrass into sagebrush ecosystems has made these ecosystems more susceptible to wildfire, which can lead to the loss of native species.
Invasive species can also have economic and social impacts on communities. In many cases, invasive species can be costly to control and manage, requiring significant resources and financial investment. For example, the control of the invasive Asian carp in the Mississippi River Basin has cost billions of dollars. Invasive species can also have negative impacts on tourism, recreation, and other industries that rely on healthy ecosystems. For instance, the introduction of the zebra mussel into the Great Lakes has led to a decline in water clarity, which can negatively impact tourism and recreational activities.
Despite the many challenges posed by invasive species, there are measures that can be taken to mitigate their impact. One approach is to prevent the introduction of invasive species through early detection and rapid response programs. These programs involve the identification and removal of invasive species before they become established in new areas. Another approach is to use biological control agents, such as predators, parasites, or pathogens, to control invasive species populations. For example, the introduction of the vedalia beetle to control the cottony cushion scale insect has been successful in California. 
In conclusion, invasive species pose a significant threat to native ecosystems, causing ecological, economic, and social problems. However, there are measures that can be taken to mitigate their impact, such as prevention, early detection and rapid response programs, and biological control.

Introduction
The Face on Mars has been a hot topic for decades, with people speculating it was crafted by aliens. But according to the article Unmasking the Face on Mars, the Face is a natural landform. My aim is to provide evidence from the article to convince anyone that the Face is just a natural landform.

Body
Claim #1: The Face on Mars is an optical illusion and is not a face.
Evidence: The author of the article states that the Face is an optical illusion that exists only in our imaginations. The author further explains that the illusion is created by shadows and the different shades of rocks on the Martian surface. 

Claim #2: The Face on Mars is a landform feature that has been eroded by weathering.
Evidence: The article states that the Face is a large, flat, featureless mesa on the Martian surface. Moreover, the author explains that the Face is eroded by the elements, such as wind, rain and ice. This erosion has caused the mesa to form shallow depressions that look like eyes and a nose. 

Claim #3: The Face on Mars is not unique and similar landforms can be found elsewhere on the planet.
Evidence: The article notes that the Face is not unique and that similar landforms can be found elsewhere on the planet. The author points out that several other mesas and buttes on Mars look like faces. This suggests that the Face is just one of many natural formations on the planet. 

Conclusion
In conclusion, it is clear that the Face on Mars is just a natural landform. The evidence from the article shows that the Face is an optical illusion created by shadows and the different shades of rocks on the Martian surface. Moreover, the Face has been eroded by weathering, which has caused shallow depressions to form. Finally, similar landforms can be found elsewhere on the planet, suggesting that the Face is not unique. Therefore, it is safe to conclude that the Face is not evidence of alien activity, but rather a natural formation on the surface of Mars.

Soccer in America: Its History, Origin, Evolution, and Popularize This Sport Among Americans Research Paper

Table of Contents
 1. Introduction
 2. Origin and history
 3. The first FIFA world cup
 4. The modern version of soccer
 5. Soccer’s popularity
 6. References

Introduction

This paper entails issues as it appertains to soccer. The coverage of the history of this game which is also popularly known as soccer is quite diverse and different ideas have been put across as to where the game originated and its evolution to the current state.

Origin and history

Soccer in America is a relatively new game when compared to other sports. Its popularity is not as in other parts of the world due to many historical factors. Other games dominate the sporting scene and only recently have there been efforts to popularize this sport among American citizens.

Different countries in the world treat soccer differently and as it turned out, it’s difficult to get one standard view on soccer or its future. Everyone who has heard about the game or who knows much about it has a personal opinion on soccer.

History holds it that many cultures played games that resembled soccer but the first format of what evolved to the modern soccer game goes way back to 3000 years ago in Japan. In Japan, a game in which a ball was kicked around a pitch, though a very small one, can be followed back to 1004 B.C. This is got from texts from way back in 50B.C that describe games played between teams from China and those from Japan. The Chinese used a leather ball that was puffed with hair and the same text explains that a soccer game between China and Japan was played in the capital of Japan in 611A.D.

The Romans also played a game that resembled soccer, though a very rough version, in the early Olympics in Rome. In this game, more than half of the players were hospitalized after the matches. It is not known as to when the sport spread from Asia to Europe since historians focused on other issues like war and tended to ignore soccer and other sports.

The impact of immigration on American identity is a complex and multifaceted topic that has been explored in literature, film, and academic discourse for decades. This exploration has provided a rich and nuanced understanding of how immigration shapes the collective identity of the United States. One such exploration can be found in Jhumpa Lahiri's novel "The Namesake," which delves into the experiences of an Indian immigrant family as they navigate the challenges of assimilation, cultural identity, and the search for belonging in America.

Lahiri's novel follows the Ganguli family, who immigrate to the United States from Calcutta, India in the 1960s. The protagonist, Gogol Ganguli, is born and raised in America, straddling the line between his Indian heritage and his American upbringing. Through Gogol's experiences, Lahiri examines the ways in which immigration shapes individual and collective identities, and how the concept of "Americanness" is constantly evolving and renegotiated in the context of cultural diversity.

One of the most significant impacts of immigration on American identity as portrayed in "The Namesake" is the tension between assimilation and preservation of cultural heritage. The Ganguli family grapples with the pressure to adopt American customs and values while simultaneously holding onto their Indian traditions and customs. This struggle is exemplified in Gogol's name, which becomes a symbol of his dual identity. His parents, Ashoke and Ashima, name him after the Russian author Nikolai Gogol, a decision that reflects their love for literature and their desire to honor their cultural heritage. However, Gogol grows up feeling alienated by his name, which sets him apart from his American peers and becomes a source of embarrassment and confusion for him. This internal conflict reflects the broader challenge faced by immigrants in reconciling their cultural roots with their desire to fit in and be accepted in their new home.

Furthermore, "The Namesake" illustrates the impact of immigration on American identity through the theme of generational differences and the evolving nature of cultural identity. As Gogol navigates his identity as a second-generation immigrant, he grapples with the expectations and values of his parents' generation while forging his own path as an American. The novel portrays the tension between the traditional, conservative values of the older generation and the more liberal, individualistic values of the younger generation. This intergenerational conflict is a common experience for many immigrant families, as the younger generation seeks to assert their unique identity while honoring their cultural roots, often leading to a redefinition of what it means to be American.

Moreover, "The Namesake" also sheds light on the impact of immigration on American identity through the lens of cultural adaptation and the formation of hybrid identities. As the Ganguli family navigates their new life in America, they undergo a process of cultural adaptation and integration, blending aspects of their Indian heritage with American customs and lifestyles. This process of cultural fusion gives rise to hybrid identities that challenge traditional notions of American identity and highlight the rich diversity of experiences and backgrounds that contribute to the tapestry of American culture. Gogol's journey of self-discovery and acceptance reflects the broader experience of immigrants who grapple with the complexities of identity, belonging, and cultural integration in their new home.

In conclusion, Jhumpa Lahiri's "The Namesake" offers a poignant and insightful exploration of the impact of immigration on American identity. Through the experiences of the Ganguli family, the novel highlights the complexities of assimilation, cultural adaptation, and the formation of hybrid identities that shape the evolving landscape of American identity. By delving into the nuances of immigrant experiences, Lahiri's novel challenges readers to reconsider the conventional narratives of Americanness and to embrace the diverse voices and perspectives that contribute to the rich tapestry of American culture. Ultimately, "The Namesake" serves as a powerful testament to the enduring legacy of immigration and its profound influence on the ever-changing fabric of American identity. It is important to recognize that the impact of immigration on American identity is an ongoing and dynamic process, shaped by the experiences and contributions of diverse immigrant communities across the nation. As the United States continues to evolve as a multicultural society, the exploration of immigration's impact on American identity remains a vital and relevant topic for further study and reflection.

In the vast tapestry of human civilization, the family structure has been a fundamental unit, the bedrock upon which societies are built and cultures are fostered. The concept of what constitutes a family, however, has morphed and evolved over millennia, influenced by myriad factors including economic conditions, religious beliefs, political ideologies, and technological advancements. This essay endeavors to explore the rich diversity and progression of family structures across various world cultures, unraveling the threads that weave the complex fabric of familial bonds.

The earliest human societies were organized around kinship networks, with family units being part of larger tribes or clans. The hunter-gatherer communities that characterized much of human prehistory relied on a communal way of life where resources were shared among members. These early societies were often egalitarian, and their family structures were fluid, with less rigid definitions of roles and responsibilities. Kinship was not solely based on blood relations but could include individuals linked by marriage, adoption, or shared goals.

With the advent of agriculture, human societies became more sedentary, giving rise to the first civilizations. This shift brought significant changes to family structures. In agrarian societies, land ownership became a critical element of wealth and power. Consequently, the family unit evolved to become more patriarchal, with inheritance typically passing through male lines. This was evident in ancient cultures such as those in Egypt, where pharaohs and nobles passed their titles and land to their sons, and in Greece and Rome, where paterfamilias, the male head of the family, held legal authority over all family members.

The concept of marriage also became more formalized during this period. Matrimonial alliances were often strategic, serving to consolidate wealth, forge political ties, or secure peace between factions. Women's roles within the family were largely domestic and centered around child-rearing and maintaining the household. The idea of romantic love as a basis for marriage was not the norm; rather, marriages were seen as practical arrangements.

The Effect of Neoliberal Policies on Global Economic Inequality

Neoliberalism is a term used to describe a set of economic policies that emphasize free markets, deregulation, and privatization. These policies have been implemented in many countries around the world since the 1970s, and have had a significant impact on global economic inequality. This paper will examine the various ways in which neoliberal policies have contributed to the widening gap between the rich and the poor, and the implications of this trend for the future of the global economy.

One of the main ways in which neoliberal policies have contributed to economic inequality is through the privatization of public goods and services. This has resulted in the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a small number of corporations and individuals, while leaving many people without access to basic necessities such as healthcare, education, and clean water. Privatization has also led to the erosion of labor rights, as corporations have sought to cut costs and increase profits by outsourcing jobs and reducing wages and benefits.

Another key aspect of neoliberalism is the deregulation of the financial sector. This has allowed banks and other financial institutions to engage in risky and unethical practices, such as predatory lending, which have contributed to the global financial crisis of 2008. The resulting economic downturn has had a disproportionate impact on the poor, who are less able to weather financial shocks and are more likely to be affected by job losses, foreclosures, and other forms of economic hardship.

Neoliberal policies have also had a significant impact on international trade and investment. The push for free trade has resulted in the movement of production to countries with lower labor and environmental standards, leading to the exploitation of workers and the destruction of local ecosystems. The globalization of the economy has also led to the concentration of wealth in the hands of a small number of multinational corporations, who have been able to use their economic power to influence governments and shape economic policies to their own advantage.

Finally, neoliberalism has had a negative impact on the ability of governments to provide for the needs of their citizens. The emphasis on fiscal austerity and the reduction of government spending has resulted in cuts to social welfare programs, education, and infrastructure, which has disproportionately affected the poor and vulnerable. This has led to increased poverty, homelessness, and social unrest, as people struggle to meet their basic needs in the face of declining public services.

In conclusion, neoliberal policies have had a detrimental impact on global economic inequality. The concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a small number of corporations and individuals, the erosion of labor rights, the financial crisis, the exploitation of workers and the environment, and the erosion of public services have all contributed to the widening gap between the rich and the poor. It is clear that these policies must be reevaluated and reformed in order to create a more just and equitable global economy.

In addressing the curiosity and fascination about studying the second planet from the Sun, this essay will explore the reasons, potential discoveries, and challenges in understanding Venus as an interplanetary companion to Earth.

Introduction

While Mars and the Moon are often the top picks in terms of interest when it comes to exploring celestial bodies, a significant amount of research and fascination also stems from Venus. The second planet from the Sun has been explored for years through various ways, be it through different types of probes, orbits, and missions. The exploration is conducted not just out of curiosity but also due to the potential discoveries that could be made and the insights it may provide us about the Earth and the Solar System as a whole.

The Driving Forces Behind Venus Exploration

Several key reasons motivate people to focus attention on Venus. First, it is a neighboring planet that closely shares properties with Earth. It serves as a valuable comparison to our planet and could provide important information about life on Earth, which in turn could help unravel mysteries surrounding the possibilities of life on other planets. Studies conducted on Venus could shed light on potential living conditions present or absent. Therefore, they hold a crucial impact on our understanding of the origin and development of life in the universe.

Second, studying Venus gives us insights into the geological history of the Solar System. The composition and characteristics of its gaseous atmosphere, the nature of its rotation, and its volcanic activity, for example, all can provide valuable data on the formation and history of our solar system millions of years ago. This can further be extended to study Earth's early development. By recognizing the similarities and differences between Earth and Venus, future research can draw meaningful conclusions about how Earth has evolved over time.

Potential Discoveries

With a comprehensive understanding of Venus, a slew of significant discoveries are likely to be made. These could encompass a wide range of topics. For instance, studying Venus' atmosphere, with its highly acidic nature and significant amount of cloud coverage, will shed light on the factors causing the variation in our planet's climate. Understanding Venus' greenhouse effect, caused by the thick atmosphere and high temperatures, may provide important insights into Earth's climatic variations too. This could be helpful in tackling significant environmental concerns, including global warming and climate change. Further, studying in detail Venus' extreme surface conditions, heat, pressure, and toxicity, could aid us in adopting new strategies to expand human exploration into extreme environments on Earth.

Another aspect to explore closely is Venus' rotational period and its magnetic field. Studying how different solar radiation levels impact the planet's surface could yield insights into the importance of a planet's magnetic field as a protective shield against cosmic radiation. 

Furthermore, one of the most fascinating aspects about Venus is the detection of phosphine gas in its atmosphere. This could be a crucial piece to understanding if life exists beyond our planet because phosphine, an organic compound, may be an indicator of microbial life on Venus. If proven, that can significantly change the perspective of life's potential in the universe.

Exploration Challenges

Exploring Venus comes with several challenges. The first and foremost of these is overcoming the harsh inhospitable environment that the probes have to encounter. The extreme temperatures, high surface pressures, and vast quantity of sulfuric acid create unique challenges in designing space exploration missions that can withstand such extreme conditions. Additionally, understanding the planet's history and its role in the early development of the Solar System would necessitate advanced analytical methods.

Another complication lies in communication between Venus and Earth when sending probes. Delays caused by these distances, along with the need for faster data transmission rates, often hamper the research process as scientists must wait for data to be received before conducting further analyses. Moreover, it is difficult to make any conclusions about how these discoveries apply to Earth solely based on the research conducted on Venus due to varying characteristics in the makeup of the planets and their respective environmental conditions.

Conclusion

In conclusion, understanding Venus is pivotal for several reasons. It allows for insightful analysis of our nearest planetary neighbor's atmosphere, the formation and evolution of our Solar System, and the potential of life on other planets. At the core, this exploration of Venus serves not only to reveal new findings about our celestial neighbor but also offers opportunities for understanding more about the Earth's formation, climatic history, and our place in the Solar System. Despite facing challenges and uncharted terrains, it remains an area of interest for many researchers and their work can contribute exponentially to future discoveries in planetary science.

Title: Car-free Cities - A Necessary Change for Sustainability

In today's rapidly evolving world, urban development continues to surge while environmental concerns grow deeper. As the popularity of car-free cities become more prevalent in discussions regarding urbanization and sustainability, it is important to consider how such models could positively impact our society and the environment, ultimately shaping our future.

Firstly, car-free cities offer a unique opportunity to mitigate pollution related to vehicular emissions. Transportation, particularly involving fossil fuels, has become a leading contributor to air pollution. When vehicles burn these fuels, they release air pollutants that can end up in the atmosphere, creating smog and harming air quality. This can lead to numerous health-related issues such as asthma, heart disease, and even premature death.

Moreover, car-free cities promote the use of more eco-friendly modes of transportation such as bicycles, public transit, and walking. These alternatives not only reduce congestion, but also promote healthy lifestyle choices, as they encourage more regular physical activity. Notably, walking and biking could decrease both the individual's risk of chronic illness and our collective dependence on the healthcare system.

Reducing the number of cars on the road would also minimize the consumption of precious resources, including fuel, steel, rubber, and concrete, all of which have negative environmental consequences when mined, processed, and used. Additionally, fewer vehicles translate to an overall reduction in the construction and maintenance of road infrastructure. With construction consuming considerable resources, this reduction would indirectly lead to environmental benefits as well, such as reducing greenhouse gas emissions from construction vehicles and the need for energy and raw materials.

The elimination of private vehicle ownership, and the implementation of car-free zones within such cities, could also have significant social implications. By removing traffic headaches, noise pollution, and visual obstructions associated with cars, public spaces could be transformed into vibrant, lively areas that are safe to use not only for pedestrians and cyclists, but also children and elderly citizens. This could foster a healthier social environment where people enjoy spending time within their communities.

Furthermore, car-free cities could encourage urban planners to prioritize greener spaces and encourage outdoor living. Instead of focusing on making cities easier to maneuver by car, these municipalities could invest more in parks, bicycle paths, and walking trails, leading to greater connections between people and green spaces. Such a shift would support biodiversity, increase mental well-being, and offer more opportunities for community engagement, which has been proven to improve overall life satisfaction.

However, adapting to such a significant cultural and infrastructural shift requires consideration of potential obstacles and how they can be overcome. Some barriers to car-free cities may include the lack of access to public transportation, higher costs associated with sustainable transportation options, and the need for adequate parking alternatives. Addressing these challenges through strategic planning, technological advancements, and ongoing partnerships with stakeholders can pave the way for a smooth transition to more sustainable transportation systems.

In summation, car-free cities present an exciting opportunity to reduce emissions, promote biodiversity, and create healthy urban environments. By encouraging more eco-friendly modes of transportation and reimagining the way cities are designed, we can create a more sustainable future that benefits both people and the planet. As our world continues to move towards a more sustainable model of urban growth, it is becoming increasingly clear that car-free cities could be a critical piece of this puzzle, offering a more environmentally responsible, healthy, and people-centric alternative to our ever-expanding urban landscape.

Design & Composition in “The Godfather” Film Essay (Critical Writing)

Table of Contents
 1. Introduction
 2. Design
 3. Composition
 4. Colors
 5. Conclusion
 6. Works Cited

Introduction

In films, the visual representation of characters and events in the context of a specific design plays a critical role in conveying a certain message and provoking emotions in the audience. The Godfather (1972), directed by Francis Ford Coppola, can serve as a vivid example of the importance of design, composition, and colors in creating the desired meaning and effect on viewers. This visual impact can be achieved by intentionally using the elements of composition and colors, focusing on the relationships between characters and moral or philosophical issues. It is possible to state that the scenes in The Godfather are built according to the principles of a compositional frame supported by a dominant color palette selected by Coppola. The purpose of this paper is to analyze how the details of design and composition as well as colors used in The Godfather contribute to accentuating relationships between characters and emphasizing moral and philosophical dilemmas.

Design

The role of design in films is to express the meaning by the visual language and composition, evoking a strong emotion in the audience. In The Godfather , some key elements of design are used to complete Coppola’s goals: differences in angles shift accents on characters, and the use of colors supports the themes of family, love, dedication, and death (Block 159). In his film, Coppola is focused on contrasts that play different roles. For example, in the scene of meeting Vito Corleone and Bonasera, Corleone’s office is shadowed, as well as the figure of Vito, to put emphasis on the power and secrets of this character in contrast to Bonasera. Furthermore, in this scene, Vito has a red rose on his lapel that contrasts with the surroundings of a dark office and attracts the viewer’s attention ( The Godfather ). In the first case, the contrast allows for thinking about differences in positions of these two men. In the second case, a red rose typically associated with a love symbol can provoke thoughts about blood.

Composition

The detailed focus on the composition of scenes in The Godfather helps to reveal the following aspects: much attention is paid to camerawork and creating different angles and perspectives. As a result, the way of how characters are set in a scene and how they are accentuated with the help of camera movement contributes to emphasizing the relationship between them (Mercado 2). For instance, in most scenes where characters communicate with Vito, they stand or sit in front of each other in dark settings, stressing tension and a possible conflict between them because of hierarchy ( The Godfather ). Thus, dark settings typical for indoor scenes highlight the importance of conversations between the characters, the content of which should not be disclosed. On the contrary, the composition of scenes that represent family members is different, and these characters tend to sit or stand on the left or right of each other, demonstrating their closeness and attachment. Color and light schemes in these scenes are brighter in comparison to scenes portraying Vito.

Colors

The prevalent color palette in the film includes black, white, dark brown, red, mahogany, and orange to accentuate key messages and moral issues. Warm colors like orange, red and mahogany can make the audience think about family and coziness of home, but in contrast, they support black in scenes where conflicting characters demonstrate violence. The used colors contradict viewers’ feelings, and they emphasize immorality of the Corleone family’s actions explained with love and benefits for all family members. Using such color effects, Coppola draws the audience’s attention to philosophical and moral dilemmas referring to the family’s well-being as the reason for making controversial decisions (Block 159). The orange-black dichotomy is represented in The Godfather in those scenes where it is important to accentuate the complexity of characters’ moral decisions as they need to choose between the good and the bad. Furthermore, Bellantoni notes that “The color flow in this film is exquisite. Never has a church been as dark for a baptism as in the baptism/slaughter sequence” (116). Thus, the color also stresses religious and philosophical issues with reference to the role of a godfather in family and society.

Conclusion

The analysis of design, composition, and colors used in The Godfather to create a certain visual effect has been presented in this paper in the context of their role in explaining relationships between the characters. The composition of scenes serves to lead the audience’s attention from one character to another depending on their hierarchy. Furthermore, it is also important to state that the use of the orange-black dichotomy supported by the palette of saturated and rich dark and warm colors contributes to representing moral dilemmas in the characters’ behavior. In the film, male characters face issues that cause them philosophically rethink their role in the family and society and make a problematic decision. Thus, it is possible to conclude that the world of the Corleone family is depicted in the film with the help of warm and dark colors in order to accentuate the ambivalent nature of their actions.

Works Cited

Bellantoni, Patti. If It’s Purple, Someone’s Gonna Die: The Power of Color in Visual Storytelling . CRC Press, 2017.

Block, Bruce A. The Visual Story: Creating the Visual Structure of Film, TV and Digital Media . 2nd ed., Taylor & Francis Group, 2017.

The Godfather . Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, performances by Marlon Brando, Al Pacino, James Caan, Richard Castellano, Robert Duvall, and Sterling Hayden, Paramount Pictures, 1972.

Mercado, Gustavo. The Filmmaker’s Eye: Learning (and Breaking) the Rules of Cinematic Composition . Taylor & Francis, 2017.

European Debt Crisis: Financial Mistakes and Solutions Essay

Table of Contents
 1. Introduction
 2. Solutions
 3. Conclusion
 4. References

Introduction

European debt crisis refers to the challenges that Europe is undergoing when paying for the debts built and accumulated over decades of financial instability.

Five of the world’s largest economies including Greece, Portugal, Ireland and Spain in one way or the other have failed to generate a stable economic growth to cater for their debts. Previously, these countries only considered challenges caused by the crisis; it is now going beyond borders and is affecting the whole world.

Europe is currently facing a serious financial crisis; debts accumulated by the member nations of European Union have raised questions about the effectiveness of European Economic and Monetary Union and what holds of euro in the coming days.

Sovereign debt is considered to be the main cause of Euro crisis. However, most of the affected countries including Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain, and other smaller economies that are linked to Euro zone, have severe monetary problems (Lynn, 2010).

The root of the crisis was a result of misallocation of resources and loss of completion within these countries. This was after the adoption of Euro about ten years ago. Currently, the economic problem is no longer the cause of the crises but a consequence brought by the changes.

The worldwide financial crisis associated with Greece raised an alarm about the debt crisis that was facing the Euro zone. The International Monetary Fund and the European Union have attempted to regain confidence in the unstable economies of Greece, Portugal and Ireland. Revealing of financial situation in Greece raised doubts on its capability to pay its debts (Kolb, 2011).

The sovereign debt that had faced these economies has continued to threaten the international monetary fund in trying to save the financial market. In addition, the spread of crisis to bigger economies like Spain and Italy poses a greater risk making the crisis more complicated.

For this reason, a lot of questions have been raised about the effectiveness of IMF and European Union. This has brought doubts concerning the future of these international monetary organizations not forgetting the fact that recovery of these debts seems futile.

Before the start of the crisis around the year 2007, the condition over the public finances was strongest over decades due to promising economic situations. The worldwide financial crisis around 2009 hit the economic activity of European countries in three different ways.

It polluted the financial system and its connectivity; it shook the confidence in wealth and demand and infected the worldwide trade actions. General preview indicated that the sub-prime lending came from US, but in the real state, the financial bodies are large in the UK and the Eurozone.

Basically the remaining financial bodies of these areas have lost considerable value. The Euro debt crisis resulted from different causes.

Some of the major causes include globalizing of money; simple loans around the year 2006 that encouraged risk lending and borrowing; worldwide imbalance of trade; monetary policies concerning government expenses and revenues and bailing out of worthless banks using private bonds (Braga & Vincelette, 2010).

Ireland banks loaned property developers without assessing their credibility. Eventually, the government was affected by the credit imbalance; it had to take all the responsibility using taxpayer’s money. There exists a connection between worldwide financial systems in that if one nation fails to pay its debts putting the outside private debt at stake, the banking system of the lending nation will experience the loss.

One of the main causes of Euro debt crisis was increasing levels of debts held by households and the governments. Around the year 1992, a treaty was signed by the European Union nations. The main agenda of the treaty was to limit the level of debts and deficit spending.

However, some members of European Union failed to abide by agreed terms of the treaty. These members operated against the regulations and ignored the world wide set limits. They used their sovereigns to shadow their debts and deficits using inappropriate means.

Complicated money exchange procedures and contradicting accounting and imbalanced final accounts characterized the initial stages of the crisis. This was accomplished by famous investment banks, and therefore, the consequences were profound.

The introduction of euro reduced interest rates on the bonds belonging to credit worthless nations. According to the IMF report, household debt levels rose from 39 % to about 138% in 2007 (Lapavitsas, 2012).

The imbalance that existed in terms of trade was another cause of Euro debt crisis. According to financial analysts around the year 2007, Germany had an improvement on its public debt and monetary deficits as compared to gross domestic product than most of other involved members of euro zone

During the same period, countries like Portugal, Spain, Ireland and Italy were at a position of paying their debts. As an improvement in trade surplus and its gross domestic product, Germany eliminated these nations out of the market making their deficits to deteriorate.

Deficit in trade also resulted in fluctuations in costs of labor. This made the nations from the south less competitive than northern nations, causing trade imbalances. Between the year 2000 and 2010, the unit of labor cost in Greece and Italy increased compared to that of Germany.

This resulted to loss of competitiveness in the labor market. European nations that have consistent surplus in trade do not realize significant change in their currency due to existence of a common currency. A high level of debt from the public is not a big issue when the government is ready to take responsibility for its debts.

The structural challenge that exists in the euro system has been a challenge a contributing factor to the Euro debt crisis. There is a union in terms of money that is known as the common currency. However, this limits economic union in terms of taxation, pension and funds activities.

Nations under Eurozone have the obligation to pursue same economic path with a different treasury to support it. In other words, nations with same financial systems are free to choose their monetary policies regarding taxes and expenditures. In this case even if there are policies about money that calls for their agreement, they may choose to reject them even if it is in the initiative of European Central Bank (Philip, 2012).

This situation brings an open ridden central economy experienced in Greece. It is difficult to make decisions concerning the monetary institutions and financial organizations. The resulting problem to the Euro zone is rampant when dealing with emergency monetary issues. With approximately seventeen members, it is difficult for the Euro zone system to make fast and rational decisions.

Inflexibility in terms of monetary policies poses a great problem to the Euro zone system, and results into a debt crisis. Member nations of Euro zone established one monetary policy that restricts them from acting independently. To be specific, they are restricted from manufacturing their own Euros to clear their debts.

This is because they use the same currency; members are not allowed to reduce its value for individual benefits, like making their exports less expensive. However, this plays a role in maintaining trade balance and raising gross domestic product. In other words, the assets that held in a currency that has reduced value will end up at a loss.

Mispricing of risks which was done about ten years before the crisis by the capital markets also contributed to the crisis. The capital markets ensured that capital was misallocated. Convergence of rates of interests along the Euro zone members that was brought by European financial union increased risk of crisis.

Euro zone is experiencing a debt crisis due to the loss of confidence. Before the growth of crisis, banks and money regulators had confidence in euro zone. Banks took extensive holdings of bonds from incapable economies like Greece, which gave little payment.

As a result of development of crisis, it became open that such economies bonds placed a greater risk to those banks. This became a center of conflict between banks due to lack of confidence in these nations (Lynn, 2010).

European financial crisis is not only economic but also political in nature. This comes from the governments responding to their deficit problems and their different interests. Leaders from European nations were found in embarrassing situation in 2010 when they had faith that crisis from payment could not stem from financial unions.

They underrated the crisis, and it has never been evaluated again. This makes surplus nations to be reluctant in endorsing them. Furthermore, resolution of crisis has been put into complication European Union legal framework. This prohibits the members of the union from assuming the debts of other members (Donovan & Murphy, 2013).

Solutions

Though European crisis is considered special because of its involvement with monetary system, it is important to come up with solutions that can be used to cope with future of the crisis. Policy makers should consider different solutions to solve the crisis.

The European crisis should consider worldwide financial integration as a way of solving the European debt crisis. However, European crisis has shown less interest in financial integration. They do not consider it as a lead to capital accumulation. During the euro era, uncontrolled financial integration resulted to unstable and weak balance of trade.

Most of European nations faced what developed nations faced ten years ago. The period is characterized with a lot of capital accumulation, which can stop suddenly. It has been repeated over for a long time. Therefore, it is important for European nations to consider a worldwide financial integration to avoid the crisis.

European debt crisis is not only affecting Europe, but it has extended beyond borders; IMF should also consider the matter of financial integration. A prevention mechanism should be designed to avoid occurrence of another crisis. It is not easy to establish such a mechanism when dealing with the crisis. However, policy makers should work closely with IMF and World Bank to solve the crisis.

European debt crisis is an indication of how fast a crisis can occur and extend to both involved and uninvolved economies. It is important to monitor and survey regional financial markets to avoid occurrence of such crisis in future.

Surveillance and monitoring will strengthen the European Union and the financial stability of its member states. When a financial crisis occurs, banks are among the most affected financial organizations.

It is important to recapitalize banks after the occurrence of the crisis. As seen from European financial crisis, banks need a clean up once they have been hit by a financial crisis. This was not achieved in Europe after their banks were hit by the sovereign debt crisis.

Conclusion

The European debt crisis has given light to major financial challenges and mistakes that have happened occurred in Euro zone. The crisis resulted from insufficient and irrational monetary policies. It would be wrong to conclude that European monetary unification was a mistake.

The political influence that enabled Greece to become a member of the European Union has had dire consequences. Ireland should have controlled its financial sector; it could have avoided its current monetary crisis.

European nations have become exposed to vulnerable conditions; an issue that requires to be addressed by policy makers. European policymakers, regardless of all denunciations, have responded to the crisis with far-reaching reforms of institutional framework, as well as structural reforms at home. However, government’s contributions are slow compared with the pace at which financial markets work.
